title: Logistic Regression II - The Sigmoid Function
abstract:
Replacing the perceptron's step function with the sigmoid is the single change
that turns a mistake-driven rule into a probabilistic model. This document covers
the formula and its shape, why the output is always between 0 and 1 however large
the input, the decision rule that converts a probability into a class, the
derivative $\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)$ that makes gradient descent possible, the
log-odds interpretation that explains the word "regression" in the name, and
the numerical-stability issues you will meet if you implement it yourself.

blocks.t: The Function
From the notes
\boxed{ \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} }

items:
Sigmoid converts the linear output of logistic regression into a
 probability between 0 and 1.

However big an input we give, the output is always between 0 and
 1.

After this we apply a decision rule: if prob $\ge0.5$, class $=1$;
 if prob $<0.5$, class $=0$.

We replaced the step function in the perceptron trick with the
 sigmoid, as the perceptron had a hard output of $0$ or $1$.

blocks.cap:
Left: the sigmoid — an S-curve squashing all of $\mathbb{R}$ into
 $(0,1)$, passing through $0.5$ at $z=0$. Middle: the step function it replaces.
 Right: the derivatives. The step's is zero everywhere; the sigmoid's is strictly
 positive, which is the whole reason for the substitution.

blocks.t: Where $z$ comes from
The linear score is exactly the perceptron's:
z = Ax_1+Bx_2+C = w^{ \top}x+b ,
so the model is
P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma \left(w^{ \top}x+b\right)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(w^{\top}x+b)}} .
Nothing about the linear part changed. Only the activation did.
Why the output is always in $(0,1)$
The proof, and the limits

For any real $z$, $e^{-z}>0$, so $1+e^{-z}>1$ and therefore
$0<\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}<1$. The bounds are approached but never reached:

\lim_{z\to+\infty}\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+0}=1,
 \qquad
 \lim_{z\to-\infty}\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+\infty}=0,
 \qquad
 \sigma(0)=\frac{1}{1+1}=\tfrac12 .

This is the notes' point: however big an input we give, the output is always
between 0 and 1. A score of $z=10^{6}$ gives a probability of essentially 1, not
of $10^6$ — which is what makes the output interpretable as a probability at all.
The symmetry

So $P(y=0\mid x)=1-\sigma(z)=\sigma(-z)$. Flipping the sign of the score flips the
class probability — which is why the two classes need only one set of weights.
The Decision Rule

blocks.cap:
Left: the fitted sigmoid, with the $0.5$ rule producing a decision
 boundary. Right: moving the threshold moves the boundary — and the threshold is
 a business decision, not a property of the model.

blocks.t: The boundary is still a straight line

The rule $\sigma(z)\ge0.5$ is equivalent to $z\ge0$, because $\sigma$ is strictly
increasing and $\sigma(0)=0.5$. So the decision boundary is
w^{ \top}x+b=0

— exactly the same linear boundary as the perceptron's. Logistic
regression is a linear classifier. The sigmoid changes what the model
outputs, not the shape of the boundary. To get a curved boundary you must
change the features (Topic 51).
$0.5$ is a default, not a law

The notes state the rule with $0.5$ because that is the natural default. It is
optimal only when false positives and false negatives cost the same. As derived
in Topic 09, the cost-optimal threshold is
t^{*}=\frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}} ,

and for imbalanced data it is often far from $0.5$. Crucially, changing the
threshold requires no retraining — it is applied to the probability
afterwards. That flexibility is the practical payoff of a soft output, and it is
what Topic 53's ROC curve is for.
The Derivative — Why the Sigmoid Was Chosen
A remarkably clean result
Write $\sigma=\sigma(z)$. Using the quotient rule on $\sigma=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$:
Now split the fraction:

= \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}
 = \sigma(z)\cdot\left(1-\sigma(z)\right)
since $\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}=1-\sigma(z)$. Therefore
\boxed{ \sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\left(1-\sigma(z)\right) }

The derivative is expressible in terms of the function's own output. During
training you have already computed $\sigma(z)$ for the forward pass, so the
gradient costs one multiplication. This is the practical reason the sigmoid became
the standard activation, and it is what makes the log-loss gradient in Topic 46 so
simple.

rows: $\sigma$ is strictly increasing, so it is invertible

blocks.t: Vanishing gradients

Because $\sigma'\le0.25$ and decays rapidly in the tails, a confidently wrong
prediction produces almost no gradient — the model learns very slowly from it.
In a deep network, multiplying many such factors together makes the gradient
vanish entirely, which is why ReLU replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers. For a
single-layer logistic regression this is not a problem, because the log-loss
gradient of Topic 46 cancels the $\sigma'$ term exactly.
The Log-Odds Interpretation
Inverting the sigmoid
Set $p=\sigma(z)$ and solve for $z$:

The quantity $\frac{p}{1-p}$ is the odds, and its logarithm is the
log-odds or logit. So the model says
\ln \left(\frac{P(y=1\mid x)}{P(y=0\mid x)}\right)=w^{ \top}x+b .
Two things this explains

items:
The name. It is called regression because it performs
 linear regression on the log-odds. It is used for classification
 because the output is converted to a probability and then thresholded.

How to read a coefficient. $\beta_j$ is the change in log-odds per
 unit of $x_j$. Exponentiating gives the odds ratio: $e^{\beta_j}$
 is the multiplicative change in the odds. A coefficient of $0.7$ means
 $e^{0.7}\approx2$ — the odds double. This is how logistic regression is
 reported in medicine and credit risk, and it is a large part of why the
 model survives despite being outperformed on accuracy.

blocks.t: Numerical Stability
Naive implementations overflow

$e^{-z}$ overflows for large negative $z$: at $z=-800$, np.exp(800) is
inf and the result becomes nan. The standard fix branches on the
sign:

Both branches are algebraically identical and neither ever exponentiates a large
positive number. scipy.special.expit implements exactly this.
Code

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import expit, logit
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Perceptron
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE FUNCTION, AND THE BOUNDED-OUTPUT PROPERTY
# =====================================================================
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

print(f"{'z':>10s} {'sigma(z)':>12s}")
for z in [-1e6, -100, -6, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 6, 100, 1e6]:
    print(f"{z:10.0f} {sigmoid(np.clip(z, -700, 700)):12.6f}")
# However big the input, the output stays inside (0, 1).

print("\nsigma(0) =", sigmoid(0))                    # exactly 0.5
print("symmetry sigma(-z) == 1 - sigma(z):",
      np.allclose(sigmoid(-np.array([1., 2., 5.])),
                  1 - sigmoid(np.array([1., 2., 5.]))))

# =====================================================================
# 2. NUMERICAL STABILITY -- the naive form overflows
# =====================================================================
try:
    with np.errstate(over="raise"):
        sigmoid(np.array([-800.0]))
except FloatingPointError as e:
    print("\nnaive sigmoid overflows:", e)

def stable_sigmoid(z):
    """Branch on the sign so we never exponentiate a large positive number."""
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    out = np.empty_like(z)
    pos, neg = z >= 0, z < 0
    out[pos] = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z[pos]))             # exp(-z) <= 1 here
    e = np.exp(z[neg])                               # exp(z)  <  1 here
    out[neg] = e / (1 + e)
    return out

extreme = np.array([-800., -50., 0., 50., 800.])
print("stable:", stable_sigmoid(extreme))
print("scipy :", expit(extreme))                     # the same, and vectorised
print("agree:", np.allclose(stable_sigmoid(extreme), expit(extreme)))

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE DERIVATIVE  sigma' = sigma * (1 - sigma)
# =====================================================================
def dsigmoid(z):
    s = expit(z)
    return s * (1 - s)                               # reuses the forward pass

eps = 1e-6
print(f"\n{'z':>6s} {'analytic':>12s} {'numeric':>12s} {'step deriv':>12s}")
for z in [-4., -1., 0., 1., 4.]:
    num = (expit(z + eps) - expit(z - eps)) / (2 * eps)
    step = (float(z + eps >= 0) - float(z - eps >= 0)) / (2 * eps)
    print(f"{z:6.1f} {dsigmoid(z):12.8f} {num:12.8f} {step:12.1f}")
# The sigmoid's derivative is non-zero everywhere; the step's is zero.
print(f"\nmaximum derivative is at z=0: {dsigmoid(0):.4f}")
print(f"in the tails it nearly vanishes: sigma'(6) = {dsigmoid(6):.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE DECISION RULE, AND WHY THE BOUNDARY IS STILL LINEAR
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
X = np.r_[rng.multivariate_normal([2, 2], [[1, .3], [.3, 1]], n//2),
          rng.multivariate_normal([5, 5], [[1, -.3], [-.3, 1]], n//2)]
y = np.r_[np.zeros(n//2), np.ones(n//2)]

m = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
w, b = m.coef_[0], m.intercept_[0]
print(f"\nw = {w.round(4)}   b = {b:.4f}")

z = X @ w + b
p = expit(z)
pred_from_prob = (p >= 0.5).astype(int)              # the notes' rule
pred_from_sign = (z >= 0).astype(int)                # equivalent
print("thresholding p at 0.5 == thresholding z at 0:",
      np.array_equal(pred_from_prob, pred_from_sign))
print("matches sklearn:", np.array_equal(pred_from_prob, m.predict(X).astype(int)))
# sigma is strictly increasing with sigma(0)=0.5, so p >= 0.5  <=>  z >= 0.
# The BOUNDARY is the straight line w'x + b = 0 -- exactly the perceptron's.

# =====================================================================
# 5. WHAT THE SIGMOID BUYS: CONFIDENCE
# =====================================================================
test = np.array([[3.4, 3.4],      # right on the boundary
                 [1.0, 1.0],      # deep in class 0
                 [7.0, 7.0]])     # deep in class 1
print(f"\n{'point':>14s} {'z':>9s} {'P(y=1)':>9s} {'class':>7s}")
for pt in test:
    zz = pt @ w + b
    print(f"{str(pt):>14s} {zz:9.3f} {expit(zz):9.4f} {int(zz >= 0):7d}")

perc = Perceptron().fit(X, y)
print("\nperceptron predictions:", perc.predict(test))
print("perceptron has no predict_proba:", not hasattr(perc, "predict_proba"))
# All three get a hard label from the perceptron. Only logistic regression
# distinguishes "barely" from "certainly".

# =====================================================================
# 6. MOVING THE THRESHOLD NEEDS NO RETRAINING
# =====================================================================
probs = m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
print(f"\n{'threshold':>10s} {'predicted 1':>12s} {'recall':>8s} {'precision':>10s}")
for t in [0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8]:
    pred = (probs >= t).astype(int)
    tp = ((pred == 1) & (y == 1)).sum()
    rec = tp / (y == 1).sum()
    prec = tp / max((pred == 1).sum(), 1)
    print(f"{t:10.2f} {int(pred.sum()):12d} {rec:8.3f} {prec:10.3f}")
# One trained model, five different operating points (Topics 48, 53).

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE LOG-ODDS -- and why it is called REGRESSION
# =====================================================================
p_ = np.array([0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9])
print(f"\n{'p':>6s} {'odds':>9s} {'log-odds':>10s} {'sigma(logit)':>13s}")
for pp in p_:
    odds = pp / (1 - pp)
    lo = np.log(odds)
    print(f"{pp:6.2f} {odds:9.4f} {lo:10.4f} {expit(lo):13.4f}")
# sigma and logit are exact inverses.
print("scipy logit agrees:", np.allclose(logit(p_), np.log(p_/(1-p_))))

# The log-odds are LINEAR in x -- verify it:
x1 = np.linspace(0, 8, 9)
grid = np.c_[x1, np.full_like(x1, 3.0)]
lo = logit(m.predict_proba(grid)[:, 1])
print("\nlog-odds differences (should be constant = w[0]):",
      np.diff(lo).round(6), " w[0] =", round(w[0], 6))

# =====================================================================
# 8. ODDS RATIOS -- how logistic regression is actually reported
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'feature':>10s} {'beta':>9s} {'odds ratio':>12s}  interpretation")
for j, bj in enumerate(w):
    orr = np.exp(bj)
    direction = "increases" if orr > 1 else "decreases"
    print(f"{'x'+str(j+1):>10s} {bj:9.4f} {orr:12.4f}  a one-unit rise "
          f"{direction} the odds by {abs(orr-1):.1%}")
# This is the form used in medicine and credit risk, and a large part of
# why logistic regression survives despite being beaten on raw accuracy.
Worked Examples
Sigmoid values, odds and log-odds
Step 1 – evaluate $\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$.
Observe that odds $=e^{z}$ exactly. Taking logs, $\log\text{-odds} = z$, which is why the linear score $z$ is called the log-odds or logit.
Step 2 – a model. Let the linear score be $z = 0.8x - 2$ for hours studied $x$. For $x=3$:
z = 0.8\cdot 3 - 2 = 0.4, \qquad P(\text{pass}) = \sigma(0.4) = 0.5987
So the model says a 59.9% chance of passing. The odds are $e^{0.4} = 1.49$.
Step 3 – the decision. Using threshold $0.5$, we predict pass because $0.5987 > 0.5$. The sigmoid is monotone, so the threshold on $\sigma$ equals a threshold on $z$ at $0$.
Derivative (needed later). $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))$. It is largest at $z=0$ (value $0.25$) and vanishes for large $|z|$, the cause of saturation in deep networks.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
$\displaystyle \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$, applied to the same linear
 score $z=Ax_1+Bx_2+C$ the perceptron used.

Sigmoid converts the linear output into a probability between 0
 and 1. However big an input we give, the output is always between
 0 and 1 — because $e^{-z}>0$ always.

Decision rule: if prob $\ge0.5$, class $=1$; if prob $<0.5$,
 class $=0$. Because $\sigma$ is increasing, this is identical to
 $z\ge0$ — so the boundary is still a straight line.

$0.5$ is a default, not a law. The cost-optimal threshold is
 $C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$, and changing it requires no retraining.

We replaced the step function with the sigmoid because the
 perceptron had a hard output of $0$ or $1$ — no confidence, and a zero
 gradient.

$\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$: expressible in the function's own
 output, non-zero everywhere, maximal ($0.25$) at $z=0$. This is what makes
 gradient descent possible.

Inverting gives $z=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}$ — the log-odds. Logistic
 regression is linear regression on the log-odds, which is why it is
 called regression, and $e^{\beta_j}$ is the odds ratio.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why is the sigmoid used in logistic regression?

Three reasons. It maps any real number into $(0,1)$ so the output can be read as a
probability. It is smooth and differentiable, so gradient descent works — unlike
the step function, whose gradient is zero. And its inverse is the log-odds, which
makes the model linear on a natural scale and its coefficients interpretable as
odds ratios.
Q. Derive $\sigma'(z)$.

$\sigma=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$, so $\sigma'=e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})^2$. Split the fraction
into $\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}=\sigma(1-\sigma)$. The
derivative is expressible in the output itself, which makes it essentially free
during training.
Q. Is logistic regression a linear model?

Yes. The decision boundary $\sigma(z)=0.5$ is equivalent to $z=0$, which is the
hyperplane $w^{\!\top}x+b=0$. The sigmoid changes the output from a hard label to
a probability, not the shape of the boundary. Curved boundaries require
transformed features.
Q. Why is it called regression if it does classification?

Because it performs linear regression on the log-odds:
$\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=w^{\!\top}x+b$. The classification comes afterwards, from
thresholding the probability.
Q. How do you interpret a coefficient of $0.7$?

A one-unit increase in that feature raises the log-odds by $0.7$, so it multiplies
the odds by $e^{0.7}\approx2.01$ — the odds roughly double. This odds-ratio form
is how the model is reported in medicine and credit risk.
Q. Should you always threshold at 0.5?

No. $0.5$ is optimal only when false positives and false negatives cost the same.
For imbalanced or asymmetric-cost problems the optimal threshold is
$C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$, chosen from a validation set — and no retraining is
needed to change it.
Q. Your sigmoid returns nan. What happened?

$e^{-z}$ overflowed for a large negative $z$. Use the sign-branching form —
$\frac{e^z}{1+e^z}$ when $z<0$ — or scipy.special.expit, which does it
for you.
